title: Ezra Leads a Group Home
overview: Ezra gathers a second group of exiles in Babylon and leads them to Jerusalem, carrying gifts for the temple and relying on prayer instead of soldiers for protection.

parts.label: Who came with Ezra (vv. 1-14)
parts.note: Ezra lists the family leaders who traveled with him from Babylon, about 1,500 men plus their families. Two priestly families and a descendant of King David head the list, tying this group to Israel's older history.

parts.label: Finding temple helpers (vv. 15-20)
parts.note: At the gathering camp by the Ahava canal, a waterway in Babylonia whose exact location is unknown, Ezra found no Levites, the tribe that assisted the priests at the temple. The text does not say why, but after he sent leaders to Iddo at Kasiphia, about 40 Levites and 220 temple servants agreed to come.

parts.label: Prayer instead of soldiers (vv. 21-23)
parts.note: Ezra had told the king that God watches over those who look to him, so asking for an armed guard felt like going back on his own words. So the group fasted and prayed for a safe journey for themselves, their children and their goods, and Ezra says God answered.

parts.label: Treasure handed to priests (vv. 24-30)
parts.note: Ezra weighed out the gifts from the king, his officials and the Jewish community and gave them to twelve leading priests, so everything could be checked on arrival. The sum was enormous, and he told the priests that both they and the treasure were set apart for God.

parts.label: The journey and arrival (vv. 31-34)
parts.note: The group left the canal in the first month and, by the dates in the previous chapter, reached Jerusalem nearly four months later without being robbed or attacked. After three days' rest the treasure was weighed again at the temple and every item recorded, showing nothing had gone missing.

parts.label: Offerings and the king's orders (vv. 35-36)
parts.note: The returned exiles offered animals burned on the altar, and the twelve bulls and twelve goats matched Israel's twelve tribes, treating this small group as standing for all Israel. The king's written orders also went to the Persian governors west of the Euphrates River, who then supported the people and the temple.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether Ezra's refusal of a military guard is a pattern of trust to imitate or simply what fit his particular promise to the king, especially since Nehemiah later accepted a royal escort.
think: When you have openly said what you stand for, how does that shape what you feel free to ask others for?
